Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am permanently an outsider now

vignette:
Marco was twenty-two when he came home from his deployment, though he felt decades older. The event itself was a single afternoon in a crowded market district-a routine patrol that collapsed into chaos when a vehicle-borne IED detonated fifty meters from his position. He remembers the pressure wave, the sound that was less a noise than a physical shove, and then the silence that followed, filled only with the ringing in his ears and the sight of a young vendor whose body had been torn apart. Marco had been trained to move toward the wounded, and he did, but when he reached the first man-a local interpreter he had shared tea with the week before-he found himself frozen. He could not remember the order of what happened next. The fragments came later, in dreams and in sudden flashes during quiet moments at his desk: the interpreter's hand reaching for him, the smell of diesel and burnt fabric, the sensation of someone pulling him backward. He could never arrange these pieces into a coherent timeline, and that confusion itself became a source of dread.

Now, at twenty-four, Marco works as a financial analyst in a high-rise office in downtown Chicago. The open-plan floor, with its glass walls and wide sightlines, makes him feel exposed. He has taken to sitting in a corner cubicle with his back to the wall, and he avoids the building's atrium during lunch. He has come to believe that he is permanently changed-an outsider among his colleagues who laugh about weekend plans and complain about quarterly reports. What frightens him most is the thought that he has no future, that the person he was before that afternoon is gone and will never return. He is certain that he acted in ways that violate who he truly is: he froze when he should have acted, and he cannot forgive himself for that failure. These appraisals press on him daily, and they drive him to avoid anything that might confirm them. He will not talk about the deployment, even when a veteran coworker tries to connect over coffee. He deleted all photos from that period and changed his route home to avoid the veterans' memorial near his apartment.

The memories themselves feed this loop. A sudden fragment-the interpreter's outstretched hand-will surface while Marco is reviewing a spreadsheet, and he will feel his chest tighten and his vision narrow. In those moments, he is certain again that he is irreparably broken, that he has no right to a normal life. This conviction then deepens his avoidance: he stops answering calls from his family, who ask when he will visit, because they remind him of the loss he carries. He has not visited his grandmother's grave since the funeral two years ago, though she raised him, because the thought of standing in the open cemetery makes him feel as though the ground might give way. His avoidance has cost him friendships; his roommate moved out last month, citing Marco's withdrawal and his refusal to explain the nightmares that wake them both.

What finally brought Marco to seek help was a performance review. His manager noted that he had missed three deadlines, that he seemed distracted, and that his usually sharp analysis had become inconsistent. Marco had not realized how much his symptoms were costing him at work. He is afraid of losing his job, but he is more afraid of what it would mean if he cannot get better-if the hopelessness he feels is not a symptom but a prophecy. He came to therapy because a part of him still hopes that the future he imagines is not the only one available to him.
